books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9; 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23: In the 1930s an extended drought struck the Great Plains, where years of over-farming had stripped the soil. Enormous dust storms ravaged parts of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, and Colorado. By the end of the decade nearly 60 percent of the farms in the region had been ruined or abandoned, and hundreds of thousands of families left, many heading for California.

rationales.A: Background from the books: most affected families abandoned their farms with little money, so buying land in California was out of reach.
rationales.B: Background from the books: many Dust Bowl refugees became migrant farmers, working on large farms growing cotton and other crops from dawn to dusk for low wages.
rationales.C: Background from the books: wartime shipyard work came a decade later, while in the 1930s Californians hired the migrants as field labor.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the FDIC, created in 1933, insured deposits in sound banks, and it employed no migrant workforce.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who moved: farm families whose land had failed.
2. Ask what they carried: almost nothing, so they could not buy land.
3. Ask what California offered them: work in the fields, for low wages.
4. They most often became migrant farm workers.
Remember: a migration story ends in a job, so ask what work waited at the other end.
